This game has helped me realize what my "niche" is...I like hacking games. After playing this, Exapunks, and TIS-100, I realized that this is the closest I am every going to get to an IT career. 

Much has been made of the term "empathy games." Hacknet qualifies as this because it makes me forget who I am for a little while. Now I am a hacker! 

I love the grind of running a porthack, taking control, cover my tracks and disconnect before the tracer finds me. There is real tension here.
Outstanding!

You are watching a street performer doing some magic tricks. You know enough that you can pinpoint all the movements and illusions right away, but still, you are enjoying the spectacle.

This is how it feel to play Hacknet if you are a software enginner. You do have a lot of fun, mostly due to excellent theming, decent writing, striking OST and feeling like a smartass. Both. In-universe: by being able to [i]Hack the World[/i] and out-universe: knowing how it’s all bullshit and understanding all the shortcuts and oversimplifications devs needed to make to create a fun experience.

For experienced in IT, this game won't be hard. Most of the "hacking" is done by just running programs in style of l33tHaX.exe in game’s version of a system console. However, for people not being too familiar with computer engineering, this definitely will be a good and educational challenge of how to use text based operating systems. Yes, I do indeed see Hacknet as a good learning tool, especially for acclimating with less user friendly interfaces.

What I think will keep the more knowledgeable people engaged is the power fantasy of being a righteous hacker on a mission. This feel is strongest with the first major faction you encounter: Entropy, which encourages more ethical approach to snooping around peoples’ PCs. Reading private conversations? Sniffing through files in places where you weren’t supposed to be? Righting some wrongs along the way? This was a desire that I didn’t knew I had and tapping into it should be  considered Hacknet’s crowning achievement. That, and few very clever setpieces game’s campaign that will keep you on your toes.

Game isn’t perfect however. I really wished that there would be more hacking-based activities that would involve more strategy, planning and logic. Solving a Firewall defenses is something a kin to what I would like to have more, but most breaching doesn’t require as much thought put into it. While writing is very good in places, there isn’t a lot of it. Story is not complicated and many computers you hack into are empty, where you would expect tons of interesting backstories and data. Game’s interface also could use some improvements, especially an unclear NetMap section.

I would definitely want to see Hacknet’s ideas improved and expanded upon in the future. This game showed me ton of potential. Some of it is unrealized for now, but I was positively surprised how much fun I had with the game, even knowing all the magic tricks and shortcuts it indulges itself in.

I believe this review to be my first, and let me say this: Hacknet is the most fun I've had with a piece of interactive media in a very long time. It oozes with immersion and masterclass functionality. After Portal 2, most people were left wandering aimlessly along the dunes of the puzzle genre. From time to time, there was an innovative incorporation of puzzle-elements, but never something so powerful. 

GNU/Linux is a UNIX-based mobile, server, office and home desktop operating system. It is built on the powerful and lightning-fast Linux kernel developed by Linus Torvalds in 1996. It's destiny was to maximize productivity and hasten the process of technological evolution. Being lightweight and monolithic, you can take Linux with you wherever you go. When you thought of the internet, you always heard about Linux ever so briefly. 

But recently, things have begun to change. As the corporation gains more control over what we've known to be the internet, people are becoming more concerned. The people want more control over what they rightfully own. Linux offers a full computer suite capable of doing everything a Windows system can do in its own way. This makes Linux a functional choice for people looking for a way out. 

To see such a beautiful piece of technology incorporated into a hacking simulator is beautiful. It's all done so faithfully too. The more I play, the more excited I get. It's fluid, only ever needing so much RAM to operate smoothly. It's also quite responsive, despite some animations taking a lot longer than they should honestly. Another minor flaw is the fact that there's no currency system. There's really only ranking as a reward. It would be cool to make some money and purchase upgrades or better tools.

My final gripe is that some of the missions get a little repetitive. But the story balances things out by keeping it all fresh. There will be funny conversations you can find throughout each system. There's also interesting hide-and-seek style treasure hunts. Listening to cyberpunk playlists really help bring the vibe forward. The interface is extremely realistic.

There was no need to go any further, everything is heavily inspired by an actual personal home desktop Linux installation. The desktop environment in this game gives me an i3-gaps vibe. I could be wrong. I'm just playing this on Linux and being amazed and how honest it feels. 

I wish you could change the wallpaper, the colors, and maybe even the font of your interface. It would make the game feel more personal and exciting. Imagine hacking on a cute hello kitty desktop! <3

If you've played and enjoyed Uplink, this is a similar game with a heavier focus on story; It is very difficult to actually lose, and you can reload your save if you do.

If Uplink doesn't mean anything to you, this is a game based around Hollywood hacking. Run programs from a very colourful terminal so you can bypass various security measures to snoop on things you weren't meant to snoop on. You do not need any real computer knowledge to play the game, though being a fast typer helps.

[Reviewing my 100%ed games by memory; please bear with me.]

I absolutely enjoyed this game. There's something about its simplistic UI that feels nostalgic, despite not growing up with adventure games made entirely in text or ASCII. Needless to say, it's very much an unconventional puzzle game; there are many times in which I got stuck, but you can try and brute-force through the puzzles... or use a guide lmao

The storytelling through the little things you can find on people's servers, computers, etc., really made it feel lived-in and interesting, and I'll admit I nearly teared up at the ending twice (I fully played it thrice for the 100%). The nonsense you can find on computers also really calls back to the simpler times of the Internet, where cringe didn't need to have layers. The grey-morality of the whole game was the icing to the cake.

Add that to the really nice soundtrack, and it's a pretty fun puzzle game with a coat of "hacker" paint on it. I'd be lying if I said that this game *didn't* influence me to learn about coding.

Easily the best hacking game since the venerable and godlike 'Uplink.' Utterly addictive, fiendishly complex (and yet paradoxically intuitive) and satisfying as all get-out. If you're looking for something where you can sit dramatically in the shadows in your hoodie, type really fast and then whisper to yourself; "I'm in," then this is for you.

It does have one or two glitches, but the experience more than makes up for it. With the excellent official expansion 'Labyrinths' and a whole host of excellent community-made extensions, there's hours of content. If you're like me, you'll find yourself still up at 4am, doing 'just one more mission.'

And remember: Trust is a weakne- oh, sorry. Wrong game.

Awesome game. I forgot about everything else going on and played this straight for a few days. The music is hands down amazing.  If you don't know how to code or use a command line, get it anyway. The commands are simple.  You can even rename your hacking programs so they are easier to type in. For example you can shorten SMTPoverflow to something easier like smtp.  And if you don't, you can also use tab auto complete (type in the first few letters of the command then hit tab - the game fills in the rest of the command."  Modding the game for new missions from the community looks super simple and the developer has held two HackerJams so far - a contest where they review and recommend community made content. Get this. Have fun.  Enjoy the music.  Finish it knowing you missed some stuff for sure and need more.
